contribution: The hydrogen energy levels $E_n = -\tfrac{13.6\,\text{eV}}{n^2}$ make spectral lines calculable: the energy of the photon from a transition is the difference between the levels, the series and absorption follow from the levels, and the Bohr model takes its place as a historical stage before the wave-mechanical model.
learn: calculate the energy and wavelength of the photon produced in a transition from the energy levels of the hydrogen atom.
explain why hydrogen emits and absorbs only certain wavelengths.
evaluate the successes and shortcomings of the Bohr model in the development of atomic models.
prior: The energy of a photon is $E = hf = \tfrac{hc}{\lambda}$, and energy can be given in electron volts (chapter *The photoelectric effect and the photon*)
The line spectrum of a gas shows that the energy of an atom can have only certain values (chapter *Spectra reveal the energy levels of atoms*)

activities.text: In a darkened classroom a thin glass tube containing hydrogen gas glows pinkish violet when a voltage is connected to it. When the light is viewed through a grating, instead of a smooth rainbow only four narrow lines are seen: red, cyan, blue and violet. The positions of the lines are always the same, whichever laboratory the tube is in.
activities.question: What in the hydrogen atom decides that it emits exactly these four wavelengths, and can they be calculated?

activities.title: Recall: the energy of a photon
activities.prompt: The hydrogen spectrum has a red line at $656\,\text{nm}$ and a violet line at $410\,\text{nm}$. Which statement about their photons is correct?

choices.text: The energy of a violet photon is greater, because the energy of a photon is inversely proportional to its wavelength.
choices.feedback: Correct. $E = \tfrac{hc}{\lambda}$ (chapter *The photoelectric effect and the photon*): the energy of a red photon is about $1.89\,\text{eV}$ and that of a violet photon about $3.02\,\text{eV}$. Today we find out where these energies come from.

choices.text: The energy of a red photon is greater, because its wavelength is longer.
choices.feedback: A longer wavelength means a lower frequency and a lower energy: $E = hf = \tfrac{hc}{\lambda}$. The energy of a red photon is about $1.89\,\text{eV}$ and that of a violet photon about $3.02\,\text{eV}$.

choices.text: The energies are equal, because both are photons emitted by the same atom.
choices.feedback: The same atom can emit photons of different energies. The energy of a photon depends on its frequency: $E = hf = \tfrac{hc}{\lambda}$, so the violet photon, with the shorter wavelength, has the greater energy.

choices.text: The photons of a brighter line have more energy, so energy depends on the brightness of the line.
choices.feedback: Brightness tells how many photons arrive per second, not the energy of a single photon. The energy of one photon depends only on the frequency: $E = hf$.

activities.title: Prediction 1: from ever higher levels to level 2
activities.prompt: The electron of a hydrogen atom falls to level $n = 2$ in turn from levels $n = 3$, $4$, $5$ and $6$. How do the wavelengths of the photons produced change as the starting level rises?

choices.text: The wavelength gets longer, because the electron falls a longer distance.
choices.feedback: The values of the model refute this: $656\,\text{nm}$, $486\,\text{nm}$, $434\,\text{nm}$ and $410\,\text{nm}$. A higher starting level means a larger energy difference, and a larger photon energy means a shorter wavelength, because $\lambda = \tfrac{hc}{E_\text{u} - E_\text{l}}$.

choices.text: The wavelength gets shorter, and successive wavelengths are ever closer to each other.
choices.feedback: The values of the model support this: $656\,\text{nm}$, $486\,\text{nm}$, $434\,\text{nm}$ and $410\,\text{nm}$. The differences decrease ($170\,\text{nm}$, $52\,\text{nm}$, $24\,\text{nm}$), because the upper levels are ever closer to each other and to zero. This is why the lines crowd together towards the series limit $365\,\text{nm}$.

choices.text: The wavelength gets shorter by the same amount each time, because the levels are evenly spaced.
choices.feedback: The values of the model refute this: the differences are $170\,\text{nm}$, $52\,\text{nm}$ and $24\,\text{nm}$. The levels of the hydrogen atom are not evenly spaced: $E_n = -\tfrac{13.6\,\text{eV}}{n^2}$, so they crowd together upwards.

choices.text: The wavelength stays the same, because the transition always ends on the same level.
choices.feedback: The values of the model refute this: the wavelength changes from $656\,\text{nm}$ to $410\,\text{nm}$. The energy of the photon is the difference between the starting and final levels, so it also depends on the starting level.

activities.title: Prediction 2: to the ground state
activities.prompt: The electron falls from level $n = 2$ to the ground state $n = 1$. What kind of radiation is produced?

choices.text: Ultraviolet radiation, because the energy difference between levels $1$ and $2$ is large.
choices.feedback: The values of the model support this: the energy of the photon of the transition $2 \to 1$ is $10.2\,\text{eV}$ and its wavelength $122\,\text{nm}$. All transitions ending in the ground state are ultraviolet, below $122\,\text{nm}$. The energy of visible-light photons is only about $1.7$–$3.3\,\text{eV}$.

choices.text: Red light, because the transition is only one level long, like the transition $3 \to 2$.
choices.feedback: The values of the model refute this: the wavelength is $122\,\text{nm}$, ultraviolet. What matters is not the difference between the level numbers but the energy difference: $E_2 - E_1 = 10.2\,\text{eV}$, whereas $E_3 - E_2 = 1.89\,\text{eV}$. The lowest levels are far apart.

choices.text: Infrared radiation, because the ground state is the lowest level and has the least energy.
choices.feedback: The values of the model refute this: the wavelength is $122\,\text{nm}$, ultraviolet. The energy of a photon is not the energy of a level but the difference between levels, and the difference $10.2\,\text{eV}$ between levels $1$ and $2$ is large.

choices.text: No radiation at all, because in the ground state the electron has stopped.
choices.feedback: The values of the model refute this: a transition produces a photon with an energy of $10.2\,\text{eV}$. Radiation comes from the transition, not from what happens in the ground state; when it drops to the ground state the atom loses energy, and a photon carries it away.

activities.title: Prediction 3: a photon that is too large
activities.prompt: A photon with an energy of $11.0\,\text{eV}$ hits a hydrogen atom in the ground state. Reaching level $n = 2$ requires $10.2\,\text{eV}$ and reaching level $n = 3$ requires $12.1\,\text{eV}$. The ionisation energy of hydrogen from the ground state is $13.6\,\text{eV}$. What happens?

choices.text: The photon is absorbed, the electron moves to level $n = 2$ and the extra $0.8\,\text{eV}$ stays with the atom as kinetic energy.
choices.feedback: The values of the model refute this: the photon of $11.00\,\text{eV}$ passes through, and photons of $10.20\,\text{eV}$ and $12.10\,\text{eV}$ are absorbed. An atom can take a photon only whole, and the energy of the photon must be exactly the difference between levels; the excess cannot be left to a bound electron.

choices.text: The photon is not absorbed but passes the atom, because its energy is not the difference between any pair of levels.
choices.feedback: The values of the model support this: $10.20\,\text{eV}$ and $12.10\,\text{eV}$ are absorbed, $11.00\,\text{eV}$ passes through, and $14.00\,\text{eV}$ ionises the atom. A bound electron can only be on the energy levels, so a photon is absorbed only if its energy takes the electron exactly to some level.

choices.text: The photon is absorbed and raises the electron to between levels $2$ and $3$.
choices.feedback: The values of the model refute this: the photon of $11.00\,\text{eV}$ passes through. There are no allowed states between the levels; the energy of a hydrogen atom can only be $E_n = -\tfrac{13.6\,\text{eV}}{n^2}$.

choices.text: The photon ionises the atom, because its energy is greater than that needed for the first excited state.
choices.feedback: The values of the model refute this: ionisation begins only at $13.6\,\text{eV}$, and the photon of $14.00\,\text{eV}$ ionises. The photon of $11.00\,\text{eV}$ passes through.

activities.text: Choose emission or absorption, set the levels and press the button. Follow the electron in the Bohr picture and in the energy-level diagram and see where the line appears in the spectrum.
activities.howto: *Situation* chooses emission or absorption. In **emission** you choose the upper level $n_\text{u}$ ($2$–$6$) and the lower level $n_\text{l}$ ($1$–$3$) and press *Transition*: the electron falls, a photon leaves, and its line stays in the spectrum strip. In **absorption** you choose the state of the atom $n_\text{l}$ and the energy $hf$ of the incoming photon and press *Send photon*. The readouts show the energies of the levels, the energy and wavelength of the photon and the result of the absorption. The spectrum strip has three parts, each with its own wavelength scale: ultraviolet, visible light and infrared. The orange triangle shows the position of the current photon. *Clear spectrum* removes the collected lines. *Speed* changes only the pace of the animation.
activities.model: The energies of the levels are the given information $E_n = -\tfrac{13.6\,\text{eV}}{n^2}$, and the zero of energy is a free electron at rest. The radii of the orbits in the Bohr picture are schematic: in the Bohr model the radius grows as $n^2$. The energy-level diagram is to scale from level $n = 2$ upwards; the gap between levels $1$ and $2$ has been shortened. In absorption the energy of the photon must equal the difference between levels to within $0.03\,\text{eV}$; the model calculates levels up to $n = 30$, although six are shown in the pictures. Close to $13.6\,\text{eV}$ the upper levels are so dense that, from the ground state, every slider value between $13.20$ and $13.55\,\text{eV}$ hits the difference of some level and is absorbed. Every photon hits an atom that is in state $n_\text{l}$. The values are calculated by the model, not measured.
activities.calc:
In emission the energy and wavelength of the photon are

$$hf = E_\text{u} - E_\text{l}, \qquad \lambda = \frac{hc}{E_\text{u} - E_\text{l}},$$

where the energy difference is converted to joules by multiplying by $1.602 \cdot 10^{-19}\,\tfrac{\text{J}}{\text{eV}}$. In absorption the model looks for a level $m > n_\text{l}$ for which $E_m - E_\text{l} = hf$. If $hf \geq -E_\text{l}$, the electron is freed, and its kinetic energy is $E_\text{k} = hf + E_\text{l}$.

activities.title: Experiment 1: the Balmer series
activities.intro: Test prediction 1. The lower level is $n_\text{l} = 2$; change only the upper level. Record the energy and wavelength of the photon for starting levels $3$, $4$, $5$ and $6$, and press *Transition* in between to see the line appear in the spectrum. Calculate how much the wavelength changes from one step to the next.

activities.title: Experiment 2: transitions to the ground state
activities.intro: Test prediction 2. The lower level is now the ground state $n_\text{l} = 1$; change the upper level and record at least the transitions $2 \to 1$ and $3 \to 1$. Which part of the spectrum strip do the lines fall in?

activities.title: Experiment 3: which photons does the ground state absorb?
activities.intro: Test prediction 3. The atom is in the ground state $n_\text{l} = 1$; change only the energy of the incoming photon. Record at least the energies $10.20\,\text{eV}$, $11.00\,\text{eV}$, $12.10\,\text{eV}$ and $14.00\,\text{eV}$ and press *Send photon* in between. The column *level after* tells which level the electron ended up on.

activities.title: Conclusion: what determines the lines?
activities.prompt: Based on your tables, write: why do the wavelengths of the Balmer series get shorter and crowd together as the starting level rises? Which photons does an atom in the ground state absorb?
activities.model: The energy of a photon is the difference between levels $E_\text{u} - E_\text{l}$. As the starting level rises, the difference grows ($1.89\,\text{eV}$, $2.55\,\text{eV}$, $2.86\,\text{eV}$, $3.02\,\text{eV}$) and the wavelength gets shorter ($656\,\text{nm}$, $486\,\text{nm}$, $434\,\text{nm}$, $410\,\text{nm}$). The differences decrease because the upper levels are close to each other. The values of the optional experiment 2 also show that the energies of transitions ending in the ground state are over $10\,\text{eV}$ and their wavelengths below $122\,\text{nm}$, so they are ultraviolet. An atom in the ground state absorbs only photons whose energy is the difference between levels ($10.20\,\text{eV}$, $12.10\,\text{eV}$), not the photon of $11.00\,\text{eV}$. A photon of at least $13.6\,\text{eV}$ ionises, and the excess stays as the kinetic energy of the electron. The values are calculated by the model from the levels $E_n = -\tfrac{13.6\,\text{eV}}{n^2}$.
criteria: I explained the change in wavelength with the energy difference of the levels and the formula $\lambda = \tfrac{hc}{E_\text{u} - E_\text{l}}$.
I justified the crowding of the lines by the upper levels being close to each other.
I said that only a photon whose energy equals the difference between levels is absorbed and that ionisation requires at least $13.6\,\text{eV}$.

activities.title: Return to your predictions
activities.prompt: Compare your predictions with the values of the model. Then return to the question at the start: why are exactly four lines clearly visible in the light of a hydrogen lamp? What happens to the transitions that end on levels $n = 1$ and $n = 3$?

activities.title: Find the error
activities.prompt:
A student calculates the wavelength of the hydrogen transition $4 \to 2$ like this:

$$\begin{aligned} &E_4 = -\frac{13.6\,\text{eV}}{16} = -0.850\,\text{eV} \\ &\lambda = \frac{hc}{0.850\,\text{eV}} \approx 1460\,\text{nm} \end{aligned}$$

The student concludes that the transition produces infrared radiation. Where is the error?

choices.text: The energy of the photon is the difference between levels $E_4 - E_2$, not the energy of a single level.
choices.feedback: Correct. The energy of the photon is $E_4 - E_2 = -0.850\,\text{eV} + 3.40\,\text{eV} = 2.55\,\text{eV}$, and $\lambda = \tfrac{hc}{2.55\,\text{eV}} = 486\,\text{nm}$, the cyan line of visible light. The energy of level $n = 2$ cannot be left out, because the transition ends on it.

choices.text: The energy should have been converted to joules; calculated in electron volts, the wavelength comes out wrong.
choices.feedback: The conversion is necessary when $h$ is in $\text{J}\,\text{s}$, but it does not fix this error: even converted correctly, $0.850\,\text{eV}$ gives $1460\,\text{nm}$. The error is in which energy is substituted.

choices.text: The energy of the level is calculated wrongly: the energy of level $n = 4$ is $-\tfrac{13.6\,\text{eV}}{4} = -3.40\,\text{eV}$.
choices.feedback: The expression divides by the square of $n$: $E_4 = -\tfrac{13.6\,\text{eV}}{16} = -0.850\,\text{eV}$ is correct. The value $-3.40\,\text{eV}$ is the energy of level $n = 2$.

choices.text: There is no error in the calculation: transitions from level $n = 4$ always produce infrared radiation.
choices.feedback: The transition $4 \to 3$ is infrared ($1876\,\text{nm}$), but the transition $4 \to 2$ is visible light ($486\,\text{nm}$) and $4 \to 1$ is ultraviolet ($97\,\text{nm}$). The wavelength depends on both levels.

activities.title: Apply to a new situation
activities.prompt: In the gas envelope of a hot star, some of the hydrogen atoms are in the excited state $n = 4$. Red light from the star with a wavelength of $656\,\text{nm}$ hits such an atom. The photon ionises the atom. What is the kinetic energy of the freed electron? Use the values $h = 6.626 \cdot 10^{-34}\,\text{J}\,\text{s}$, $c = 2.998 \cdot 10^{8}\,\text{m/s}$ and $1\,\text{eV} = 1.602 \cdot 10^{-19}\,\text{J}$. Answer in electron volts.
hints: First calculate the energy of the photon in electron volts and the energy of level $n = 4$. How much energy does freeing the electron from this state require?
The electron rises from the level $E_4 = -\tfrac{13.6\,\text{eV}}{16}$ to the energy zero, and the rest of the photon's energy stays as kinetic energy: $E_\text{k} = hf + E_4$.

$hf = \dfrac{hc}{\lambda} = \dfrac{1.9865 \cdot 10^{-25}\,\text{J}\,\text{m}}{656 \cdot 10^{-9}\,\text{m}} = 3.0282 \cdot 10^{-19}\,\text{J}$; convert this to electron volts and add $E_4 = -0.850\,\text{eV}$.

mistakes.feedback: This is the whole energy of the photon. Part of it is used to free the electron from state $n = 4$: $E_\text{k} = hf + E_4 = 1.89\,\text{eV} - 0.850\,\text{eV}$.
You added the binding energy to the energy of the photon. Freeing the electron uses up energy: $E_\text{k} = hf - 0.850\,\text{eV}$, because $E_4 = -0.850\,\text{eV}$.

activities.solution:
**Given:** atom in state $n = 4$, $E_n = -\tfrac{13.6\,\text{eV}}{n^2}$, wavelength of the light $\lambda = 656\,\text{nm}$, $h = 6.626 \cdot 10^{-34}\,\text{J}\,\text{s}$, $c = 2.998 \cdot 10^{8}\,\text{m/s}$ and $1\,\text{eV} = 1.602 \cdot 10^{-19}\,\text{J}$

**Asked:** the kinetic energy $E_\text{k}$ of the freed electron in electron volts

**Principle:** In ionisation the electron rises from the level $E_4$ to the energy zero, and since a free electron has no levels, the energy of the photon does not have to be a difference between levels; the excess stays as kinetic energy. Energy is conserved, so $hf + E_4 = E_\text{k}$.

**Formula:** $hf + E_4 = E_\text{k}$ and $hf = \dfrac{hc}{\lambda}$, so

$$E_\text{k} = \frac{hc}{\lambda} + E_4$$

**Conversions:** $\lambda = 656\,\text{nm} = 656 \cdot 10^{-9}\,\text{m}$; the energy of the photon is converted from joules to electron volts by substituting $1\,\text{eV} = 1.602 \cdot 10^{-19}\,\text{J}$.

**Substitution:** $hf = \dfrac{6.626 \cdot 10^{-34}\,\text{J}\,\text{s} \cdot 2.998 \cdot 10^{8}\,\text{m/s}}{656 \cdot 10^{-9}\,\text{m}} = 3.0282 \cdot 10^{-19}\,\text{J} = \dfrac{3.0282 \cdot 10^{-19}}{1.602 \cdot 10^{-19}}\,\text{eV} = 1.8902\,\text{eV}$. $E_4 = -\dfrac{13.6\,\text{eV}}{16} = -0.850\,\text{eV}$. $E_\text{k} = 1.8902\,\text{eV} - 0.850\,\text{eV} = 1.0402\,\text{eV}$

**Answer:** $1.04\,\text{eV}$, three significant figures, as in the wavelength $656\,\text{nm}$ and the value $13.6\,\text{eV}$.

**Reasonableness:** The kinetic energy is positive and smaller than the energy of the photon, $1.89\,\text{eV}$, as it should be. From the ground state the same red photon would not ionise, because that requires $13.6\,\text{eV}$: in a high excited state the electron is so weakly bound that visible light is enough.

activities.text: Practise on three levels. The tasks of level 1 use one formula, those of level 2 combine the energies of the levels and the wavelength of the photon, and level 3 requires reasoning in a new situation.

activities.title: 1. Concept
activities.prompt: The energy of the ground state of the hydrogen atom is $-13.6\,\text{eV}$. What does the negative sign mean?

choices.text: The electron is bound: freeing it from the atom requires $13.6\,\text{eV}$ of energy.
choices.feedback: Correct. The zero of energy is a free electron at rest. The energy of a bound electron is lower than this, and the difference $13.6\,\text{eV}$ is the ionisation energy.

choices.text: The electron has negative kinetic energy, because it moves towards the nucleus.
choices.feedback: Kinetic energy cannot be negative. The energy of a level is the sum of kinetic and potential energy relative to a free electron, and it is negative because the electron is bound to the nucleus.

choices.text: The atom has lost $13.6\,\text{eV}$ of energy, so it is missing energy.
choices.feedback: A negative value does not mean a shortage but the chosen zero: energy is measured from a free electron. The ground state is a stable state, not a deficient one.

choices.text: The charge of the electron is negative, and the energy gets the same sign as the charge.
choices.feedback: The sign of the energy does not come from the charge. It comes from the choice of zero: the energy of a free electron is zero, and the energy of a bound electron is lower than that.

activities.title: 2. The wavelength of a transition
activities.prompt: The electron of a hydrogen atom moves from level $n = 5$ to level $n = 3$. Calculate the wavelength of the photon produced, when the energies of the levels are $E_n = -\tfrac{13.6\,\text{eV}}{n^2}$. Use the values $h = 6.626 \cdot 10^{-34}\,\text{J}\,\text{s}$, $c = 2.998 \cdot 10^{8}\,\text{m/s}$ and $1\,\text{eV} = 1.602 \cdot 10^{-19}\,\text{J}$. Answer in nanometres.
hints: The energy of the photon is the difference between levels $E_5 - E_3$, not the energy of either level.

mistakes.feedback: You used the energy $0.544\,\text{eV}$ of level $n = 5$ as the energy of the photon. The energy of the photon is the difference between levels $E_5 - E_3 = 0.967\,\text{eV}$.
You used the energy $1.51\,\text{eV}$ of level $n = 3$ as the energy of the photon. The energy of the photon is the difference between levels $E_5 - E_3 = 0.967\,\text{eV}$.

activities.solution:
**Given:** upper level $n = 5$, lower level $n = 3$, $E_n = -\tfrac{13.6\,\text{eV}}{n^2}$, $h = 6.626 \cdot 10^{-34}\,\text{J}\,\text{s}$, $c = 2.998 \cdot 10^{8}\,\text{m/s}$ and $1\,\text{eV} = 1.602 \cdot 10^{-19}\,\text{J}$

**Asked:** the wavelength $\lambda$ of the photon in nanometres

**Principle:** Energy is conserved: the energy of the atom decreases by the difference between the levels, and one photon, with energy $\tfrac{hc}{\lambda}$, carries it away.

**Formula:** $\dfrac{hc}{\lambda} = E_5 - E_3$, so

$$\lambda = \frac{hc}{E_5 - E_3}$$

**Conversions:** $E_5 - E_3 = -\tfrac{13.6\,\text{eV}}{25} + \tfrac{13.6\,\text{eV}}{9} = 0.96711\,\text{eV} = 0.96711 \cdot 1.602 \cdot 10^{-19}\,\text{J} = 1.5493 \cdot 10^{-19}\,\text{J}$; finally $1\,\text{m} = 10^{9}\,\text{nm}$.

**Substitution:** The product $hc = 6.626 \cdot 10^{-34}\,\text{J}\,\text{s} \cdot 2.998 \cdot 10^{8}\,\text{m/s} = 1.9865 \cdot 10^{-25}\,\text{J}\,\text{m}$. $\lambda = \dfrac{1.9865 \cdot 10^{-25}\,\text{J}\,\text{m}}{1.5493 \cdot 10^{-19}\,\text{J}} = 1.2822 \cdot 10^{-6}\,\text{m} = 1282.2\,\text{nm}$

**Answer:** $1.28 \cdot 10^{3}\,\text{nm}$, that is about $1280\,\text{nm}$, three significant figures, as in the value $13.6\,\text{eV}$.

**Reasonableness:** The transition ends on level $n = 3$, so it belongs to the Paschen series and is infrared. The wavelength is within the range of the series, $821$–$1876\,\text{nm}$, and shorter than the wavelength $1876\,\text{nm}$ of the transition $4 \to 3$, because the energy difference is larger.
activities.practice: Practise calculating the difference between levels in the tasks of level 2.

activities.title: 3. The Bohr model
activities.prompt: The Bohr model is called a stage in the history of atomic models. What did the model explain correctly, and why has it been given up? Answer in three or four sentences.
activities.model: The Bohr model explained why hydrogen emits and absorbs only certain wavelengths: the electron can only be on allowed orbits, and the energy of a photon is the difference between the energies of the orbits. The energy levels of hydrogen obtained from the model, $E_n = -\tfrac{13.6\,\text{eV}}{n^2}$, agree with the measured spectral lines and the ionisation energy. However, the model does not work for atoms with more than one electron, and it does not explain the differences in the brightness of the lines. In addition, the electron has no observable orbit; the wave-mechanical model describes the position of the electron with probabilities but keeps the energy levels.
criteria: I name at least one thing the model explained correctly: the line spectrum of hydrogen, the energy levels or the ionisation energy.
I name at least one shortcoming: atoms with many electrons, the brightnesses of the lines or the lack of an orbit in reality.
I say what the new model keeps (the energy levels) and what it gives up (the orbits).

activities.text: Finally, two quick questions. Answer first yourself and open the answer only then.
